Establish a foundation in research related to embedded system analysis, design, and synthesis. Lectures, assigned reading, and student presentations used to survey fundamental embedded systems topics. The second half-semester focuses on an important and timely research topic. Survey-only (3 credit) and project (4 credit) versions.

Advanced topics in computer vision. Topics are selected from large-scale vision and language foundation models, generative methods such as denoising diffusion and energy-based models, discriminative methods such as contrastive learning and few-shot classification, neural net architectures, model optimization and compression, current research on recognition, detection, segmentation, tracking, inferring depth, reconstructing scenes in 2D, 3D, and 4D, multimodal perception and robotics.

Fundamentals of supervised, unsupervised, and sequential learning, including linear and nonlinear regression, logistic regression, support vector machines and kernel methods, decision trees, ensemble methods, neural networks and deep learning, dimension reduction, clustering, and probabilistic models. Emphasis on algorithms and their derivation from fundamental principles.  Includes applications to real-world data. Projects are overseen/graded by faculty and may also involve mentoring by representatives from external organizations.

Geometry, kinematics, differential kinematics, dynamics, and control of robot manipulators.  The mathematical tools required to describe spatial motion of a rigid body will be presented in full.  Motion planning including obstacle avoidance is also covered.

Architecture for explicit parallelism.  Multithreaded processors, small- and large- scale multiprocessor systems.  Shared-memory coherence and consistency.  Effect of architecture on communication latency, bandwidth, and overhead.  Latency tolerance techniques.  Interconnection networks.  Case studies.  Term projects.

In this course, students develop confidence and fluency communicating in English in and outside the classroom. They practice interactive speaking skills and learn to understand the cultural foundations of language and communication in academic situations such as seminars, meetings with professors, and collaboration with classmates.

After an initial meeting, this course can be taken entirely online. Students enhance their English vocabulary for reading, writing, speaking, and listening. They develop strategies to be able to report content in their own words and to actively participate in class. Optional in-person gatherings provide support and community-building.

In this course, students develop their English writing skills for their university coursework and for professional situations such as internships. They learn how to identify academic and professional writing patterns and how to draft, revise, and polish written assignments that effectively communicate their ideas.

This class equips students to enhance their ability to be understood, whether on campus or in the larger community. Students identify the features of pronunciation that can maximize clarity and practice these features to make them more automatic.

Course topics vary. This course concentrates on skills in English for academic purposes such as speaking, listening, reading, writing, grammar, and pronunciation. The format of these courses, scheduling, and patterns of assessment will vary according to the instructor.

Course topics vary. This course concentrates on skills in English for academic purposes such as speaking, listening, reading, writing, grammar, and pronunciation. The format of these courses, scheduling, and patterns of assessment will vary according to the instructor.

Students prepare to teach English in an international setting. Students learn and use best practices in EFL pedagogy. Students learn how to develop appropriate materials and resources for an engaging and interactive communicative classroom, and how to employ these materials in various contexts.

Students will pursue individual research on a wide variety of topics related to second language acquisition, teaching or learning. Research projects would be completed done under the supervision of ELI faculty, who should be consulted as to possible topics or ongoing projects in which students could participate.

This class is about writing and academic inquiry, with a special emphasis on literature. In this writing-intensive course, students focus on the creation of complex, analytic, well-supported arguments addressing questions that matter in academic contexts.
In this writing-intensive course, students focus on the creation of complex, analytic, well-supported arguments addressing questions that matter in academic contexts.

This course serves as an introduction to writing for academic and non-academic communities in a stance of self-reflection, humility, and respectful listening. Through collaboration with the Edward Ginsberg Center, the class will collaborate with a community partner and practice applied, community-engaged writing.

A course in the LSA First-Year Seminar Program taught by a faculty member.  Course involves focused study of selected topics in English language and literature through classroom discussion and the writing of essays.
This course serves as an introduction to Shakespeare's works. Students will gain familiarity with historical context and scholarly discussions around his plays and poems.
This course introduces students to the study of English language and literature through lecture and discussion. Courses explore a broad range of topics across historical periods, genres, and themes.

This course introduces students to critical tools and concepts useful to studying literature and other forms of expression from across cultural and ethnic groups in North America. The course will deepen student understanding of multiple perspectives about race and ethnicity in America as well as the representation of various identities.

In introductory ways, students engage the scope, patterns, influence, and power of linguistic and rhetorical events and structures in a variety of contexts. Goals for the course include increasing critical thinking and deepening an awareness of the situational dynamics of language use.

This course introduces students to a range of literature's written by LGBTQ (lesbian, gay, transgender, and queer) writers as well as by writers speaking from identities embraced by broader definitions of community (queer, intersex, allied) and/or writers that engage with questions of gender, sex and sexuality, identity, and politics.

This course surveys literary works written by women and introduces students to basic literary-critical or rhetoric-based reading methods. Courses may focus on a group of women writers defined by a period, a literary form or rhetorical tradition, or on representations of women in a range of literatures.

This course provides a basic understanding of critical ideas and interventions of the field of Disability Studies. Students explore ways of knowing, relating, and moving in mind of physical and cognitive disability, encouraging understanding of accessibility as a lived practice that generates insights about the digital and physical world around us.

This course combines the study of literature and writing by focusing on non-classroom-based literary activities. Students can expect to learn with literary texts and explore reading and writing in local or non-academic communities.

This course introduces students to the craft and critique that characterizes creative writing as a discipline and profession. Focusing on two genres of writing (e.g. poetry and fiction), this course treats creative writing as a skill and a habit of mind that students can actively develop.

This course builds upon skills from introductory writing courses and focuses on the presentation, explanation, and assessment of claims through written reasoning that utilizes appropriate evidence and writing conventions.

A creative writing course in the rudiments of playwriting. Students will explore plot/action, conflict, character, and other elements. Students will create a series of short plays through specific writing exercises.

This course focuses on the genres typically encountered in professional workplace writing environments, such as technical instructions, memos, reports, proposals, correspondence, and application materials, and it addresses ethical issues that arise in professional communication.

This course explores artful works of prose that blossom with meaning and style when studied and discussed. Readings may focus on fiction (novels, short stories), non-fiction (memoir, travel writing, essay), or a combination of both. Students will learn basic interpretive terms and methods.

This course offers a broad introduction to the field of visual culture and visual rhetorics. Students will learn methods for studying the techniques and themes of graphic narrative and comics, photography and illustration, film, internet memes, and other visual texts/media.

This course introduces students to the rich tradition of Jewish storytelling. We explore diverse approaches to storytelling, including rabbinic Midrash, Hasidic tales, and modern short stories. Particular attention is paid to the role of storytelling in response to historical displacement and trauma.

This course explores the basic conventions and questions of autobiography and/or life writing. How is the self's story told? Why does it matter what is actual and invented? How does life give shape to narrative?

This course introduces students to basic methods, terminology, and questions relevant to understanding poetry. Offerings explore poems originating from both the past and present as well as observing forms both conventional and experimental.

This course is organized around interdisciplinary approaches to topics in English literature and language, where literary expression and interpretive methods are studied alongside the methods of, for example: economics, natural science, history, philosophy, medical humanities, and others.

This course explores the history, theory, and craft of literary journalism, a long-standing literary genre that includes personal essays, profiles, and immersive investigations of the social landscape. Students will examine the origins of literary journalism, analyze well-known and influential examples of the genre, and experiment with using its characteristic devices in writing their own nonfiction narratives.

This course focuses on a form, genre, period, movement, author, or special topic in the history of drama and/or performance. Because the course is open to all students, it includes introductory material in the study and interpretation of dramatic or performance-based art.
Literary genres of the Old and New Testaments and the formation of the Canonical Book.

This course offers an introduction to studying literature from Britain and/or its sphere of linguistic and cultural influence, including literature from Ireland as well as former colonies of the British Empire. Offerings explore a variety of social and historical contexts and themes.

Horror, fantasy, romance, detective/noir fiction, true crime, science fiction: this course introduces students to "genre fiction," stories that use particular features of storytelling which, because highly recognizable to readers and often developed through serialization, foreground expectation and lore as sources of meaning.
This lecture course includes Shakespearean and non-Shakespearean drama. It also includes other literary genres from sixteenth and seventeenth century England.
This course offers a broad introduction to American literature. Students engage texts from a wide range of the literary-historical contexts of North America from various periods.

This course surveys literature composed in English from around the world, focusing primarily on those composed outside the US/UK. Students learn basic terms/concepts useful to understanding literature in a world/global framework as well as particular national/cultural contexts useful to studying literature outside of our own North American context.
Courses taught under this number take a thematic approach to language and literature.
Classes taught under this number are low credit or mini courses with varying topics.
Concentrated study of a single major literary work.

Examines the consequences of language use in the world in which we live from the persuasive effects of rhetorical strategies, to the relationship between linguistic practices and literary form, to the political consequences of disputed as well as shared literary and literacy practices across different discourse communities.

Students practice using two or more analytical approaches or interpretive frameworks for studying literature (e.g., feminist theory + critical race studies; ecocriticism + historicism). Courses may include study of non-literary arts/forms of expression, a general or thematic approach, and bibliographic research or extracurricular activities for exploring methods.

The phonemic and grammatical structure of present-day English considered in the light of modern linguistic science, with some attention to problems of usage, word formation, meaning, and changes in meaning.
A historical survey of the sounds and structures of the English language from 900 to the present time with particular emphasis upon the language of Chaucer and Shakespeare.
This course explores how political theater affects and is affected by current trends in American politics.
This course considers various thematic approaches to literature and will be organized around texts and concepts raised by a particular set of authors, historical period, or genre.
A broad survey of a major literary or cultural theme, focusing on gender and/or sexuality as categories of analysis central to the understanding of human life and society.

Courses may focus on a group of women writers defined by a period, a literary or rhetorical tradition, or on representations of women in a range of literature. Study is informed by critical frameworks (such as feminist politics or gender theory) and histories of women's every day and extraordinary lives.

This course introduces students to the range of texts, themes, and conceptual terms that constitute disability studies approaches to poetry, novels, creative nonfiction, dance, theater and the visual arts.

This course focuses on literary readings that recreate a sense of a specific culture, e.g. English Renaissance, Beat Literature, Revolutionary Ireland, South African Apartheid (English-speaking). Content varies from term to term.

This course studies a set of readings bound together by their similarity on the structural or modal levels, both genre (such as Epic, Romance, Satire, Lyric Poetry, Tragedy, etc.) and genre fiction (such as horror, detective/noir fiction, true crime, historical, etc.).

This course studies the effect of scientific, economic, political, or cultural change upon literature, with particular reference to the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.  Some of the topics which may be offered include science and poetry, or politics and the modern novel; or the focus may be on a particular theme, for example, urbanization and the theme of alienation in modern literature.

This course studies a variety of literary texts that respond to nature and wilderness and thinks through concerns about management, environmental degradation, planetary extinction, and concepts of sustainability.
This independent study allows students to engage in internship placements throughout the academic year and apply their experience to their English studies.
This course combines two components: an internship position in community journalism and a writing seminar that supports students as they produce written work related to their internship positions.

This course offers students practice in writing original fiction. Courses are structured through workshop, that is, regular sharing of your draft work, peer commentary, revision, and instructor feedback.

This course offers students practice in writing original poetry. Courses are structured through workshop, that is, regular sharing of your draft work, peer commentary, revision, and instructor feedback.
This course focuses on examining and practicing artistic and research-informed essay writing, or shorter compositions that employ stylistic devices from multiple genres to develop a point of view.
Practice in writing short plays.  Conceptualizing a full-length play.

Students in this course write essays -- descriptive, narrative, argumentative, even ones that might be strongly advocating a particular position -- that grow out of knowledge or curiosity about the natural world. We also read examples of environmental writing, literary and scientific, that may be used as models or inspiration.

The various sections of this course are devoted to concentrated analysis of particular directors or of particular schools of filmmaking.  Representative films are shown and discussed in terms of their place in the context of film history.  General theoretical concepts about film are developed.
This course offers study in techniques and themes of visual texts/media, including graphic narrative and comics, photography and illustration, and film.

This course explores how biography and creative non-fiction tell life stories in new ways, using multiple forms of evidence, narrative, and media to challenge expectations about how we live in our world.

This course examines how the Bible became a physical book, a material object, that can be held in the hands. Topics include ancient technologies such as scrolls and codices, medieval manuscripts, the printing press, 18th-19th century Bible production, and contemporary employment, in films, museums, the arts, and the digital revolution.
This course studies and analyzes poetry using various topics and themes. Students write, critique, and formulate responses to poetry.

Fantasy is a literary genre steeped in magic, the supernatural, and both invented and existing folklore and history. This course explores forms of fantasy in literature and uses of the fantastic in visual and verbal art forms across time.

In science fiction and speculative fiction, writers explore alternative worlds and possible futures that reflect if not arise from our own. This course explores science fiction and speculative fiction in stories, novels, and film.

This course give students the basic research and writing skills to cover emerging issues related to the environment and public health.  Students learn to produce journalistic writing, which differs markedly from academic writing.  The emphasis is on communicating to a wide audience.  Students also become more savvy news consumers

The course assists students in using their college and academic writing skills to practice producing publishable writing, giving attention to publishing contexts both print and digital. Course themes will vary by instructor, and range across topics such as journalism, creative nonfiction, organizational blogging, and publicity writing.

This course offers study of drama/theatre studies and/or performance studies. Students study theoretical framings and traditions and explore questions relevant both to everyday life and to understanding imaginative/creative events, practices, and texts.
A course designed to give students a strong understanding of the range of literary works in English to 1660.
A course designed to give students a strong understanding of the range of literary works written in English from 1830 to the present.

This course concerns the growth of the US novel from the early national period to the present. It investigates both what the US novel shares with other American-continental and Anglophone novel traditions as well as its unique responses to US historical and social conditions. Courses typically investigate major authors (Henry Melville, Edith Wharton, Zora Neale Hurston, William Faulkner) alongside lesser-known and emerging writers.

Modern novels focus on the experience of life as alienated and/or liberated from traditional belief systems, communities, and ways of knowing, and exploit long-form storytelling as a way to capture that experience. This course studies several major modern novels from the period of its flowering in the early and mid 20th centuries by writers such as Henry James, James Joyce, Virginia Woolf, and James Baldwin.
This course studies a selection of Shakespeare's plays to increase student's critical appreciation and understanding of the playwright's art and thought.
Survey of the written works and historical context of major writer Jane Austen.

This survey course introduces students to a broad range of texts, in English, written in or about the Americas.  Topics vary each term and may be limited to U.S. texts or may include texts (in translation) that cross current national borders but represent a comparable aesthetic, conceptual, or social response to a shared experience or moment in history.

Primarily literature composed outside of the US/UK and written in critical relation to imperial/colonial projects of western modernity. Students will develop their understanding of English as a world language and global literature in light of theories and histories of colonialism and decolonization, translation, and transnational literary circulation.

This course considers a range of topics in the study of Jewish literature.  It raises questions concerning the canon of texts studied, the cultural construction of Jewish literature, race and ethnicity.
Course in specific topics pertaining to literary criticism and theory. Content and emphasis varies from term to term.

This is one of three New England Literature Program (NELP) courses. This course represents the program's intensive study of literature as part of the culture of the New England region and North America more broadly. Topics include transcendentalism, Native American folk lore, and American poetry of the nineteenth through the twenty-first century.

This is one of three New England Literature Program (NELP) courses. This course represents the program's intensive study of literature as engaging with the natural environment of New England and of the environmental humanities. In addition to studying nature writing, nature poetry, and folk lore, students will explore topics such as environmentalism, industrial impacts on wilderness, and indigenous conceptions of ecology.

This seminar prepares students for writing a research project. It includes study of research methods, literary criticism, and writing techniques. Period and topic will vary depending on the instructor's expertise. Requirements may include independent research, intensive readings, oral presentations, annotated bibliographies, and critical writing.
This seminar educates students in advanced writing methods for discussing literary texts and issues in literature and or language. Students will produce and share significant writing projects.

This course, part of the New England Literature Program, focuses on intensive writing through handwritten journal entries. Without electronics, students share and revise academic and creative work based on readings. Emphasis is placed on clarity, genre, and audience. Students complete 150-400 pages of writing by course end.

This course examines the consequences of language use, its persuasive effects, linguistic and literacy practices, literary forms, and political manifestations within specific time periods, topics, and/or discourse communities.  Topics vary by term and instructor.

An introduction to some of the major theories that shape approaches to written composition.  Investigation of how such theories shape practices, especially the classroom practices of writing teachers.
This class considers the various critical approaches to literature, either by direct study or by application to a particular writer, period, or genre.

This course examines topics such as American English, English as a world language, and dialects in English. It also studies the ways speech reflects our personal views about national and regional origins, race, class, ethnicity, religion, age, gender, and sexual orientation.
This course provides an intensive introduction to Old English, both its grammar and lexicon, in order to allow students to begin to read and translate Old English texts.

This course provides an intensive introduction to Middle English in order to allow students to read and translate Middle English texts.  The course covers Middle English grammar and lexicon, as well as the dialect variation that characterizes texts from this period.

A detailed examination of a specific literary of cultural topic pertaining to gender and/or sexuality, exploring such issues as the relation between social identity and aesthetic form, sex and politics, gender and history.

This course offers study of a special topic on women and literature. Courses may focus on a group of women writers defined by a period, a literary form or rhetorical tradition, or on representations of women in a range of literatures.
This course offers study of graphic narrative, including Comic Books, Graphic Novels, and Sequential Art.

This advanced course offers students practice in writing original fiction. Courses are structured through workshop, that is, regular sharing of your draft work, peer commentary, revision, and instructor feedback.

This advanced course offers students practice in writing original poetry. Courses are structured through workshop, that is, regular sharing of your draft work, peer commentary, revision, and instructor feedback.
Practice and guidance in the writing of expository prose, primarily for students at work on long papers, with special attention in conference to individual writing problems.

Students write a dramatic text, complete a series of assigned technique exercises and material reading, participate in class discussions and live readings, leading to the completion of a Full-Length play.

This course is a creative writing tutorial for students who have been accepted into the Capstone Program in Creative Writing. In this course, students complete a major manuscript of fiction or poetry. Includes supervised reading and writing assignments and regular tutorial meetings with faculty.
This course centers on a craft-based approach to understanding literature, that is, on the questions, objectives, and techniques of practicing creative writers in composing their works.
This course offers in-depth exploration of a specific poetic movement, genre or sub-genre, or critical questions in the field of poetry and poetics over the 20th and 21st centuries.
This course examines a special topic within the field of poetry and poetics.
A course which ranges widely (by genre or theme) over literature in English to 1660.
Focusing on a special topic such, this seminar gives students a strong understanding of literature in English from 1830 to the present.
This course addresses specific issues or trends in the history of the novel. Examples include unreliable narration in the novel form, the post-colonial novel, and the gothic novel then and now.
Course is in the works of a major author.
This course is an intensive study of Chaucer's major works. It includes reading in Middle English and background lectures covering many tales.
This course is designed to consider specific issues and approaches to Shakespeare's work for students who have already gained some basic familiarity with his texts.
This course is designed to consider specific issues and approaches to John Milton's work.

This seminar on American literature focuses on a topic from the colonial period through the contemporary. Students engage texts from a wide range of the literary and historical contexts of North America.

This seminar offers thematic study of the critical field known as postcolonial studies. Courses examine literature from around the world that explores fundamental questions concerning empire, colonialism, race, alterity, nation, decolonization, translation, diasporic and transcultural study. Courses may take postcolonial approaches to understand literature from any historical period.

This course provides an in-depth study of a variety of topics in Disability Studies, including architectural design, education/pedagogy, social movements, political activism, engineering, health sciences, and arts practice and study. Disability Studies takes a critical perspective on medical, curative, and individualist frameworks for understanding disability and aims to practically intervene in the material/social world.
Students develop the prospectus and first draft of their honors thesis during this course taken during the Fall Term of the Senior year with the final thesis submitted in March.
Students develop the final draft of their honors thesis during this course taken during the Winter term of their senior year.

This is a survey course of the basic numerical methods which are used to solve scientific problems. In addition, concepts such as accuracy, stability and efficiency are discussed. The course provides an introduction to MATLAB, an interactive program for numerical linear algebra as well as practice in computer programming.
This performance course may fulfill requirements for certain majors and minors.

An SMTD outreach ensemble in partnership with the Prison Creative Arts Project. Students will perform and lead workshops in prisons, community and youth detention centers. Undergraduate, graduate, U-M alumni and community members for PCAP program are allowed to audition and participate in this ensemble.
This mini-course addresses topics concerning weather and climate factors, specifically how climate affects humans and how humans affect climate.
Seminar on environmental topics for first-year students.
This introductory level special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a social science perspective. Specific social science topics will vary by term.
This introductory special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a humanities perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This introductory special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from an interdisciplinary perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.

This course melds student research and hands-on action. Topics are focused on environmental sustainability concepts related to the world, personal lives, and the University of Michigan campus. Students will develop sustainability literacy and evaluate their decisions and practices (individually and as teams) to address sustainability issues with action on campus.

How have you interacted with your environment today? The environment impacts your life in more ways than you might think! This course involves lectures and discussions on ecological principles and concepts underlying the management and use of natural resources. The class emphasizes the importance of interdisciplinary approaches to matters concerning the allocation of natural resources and the quality of our environment. We will track production and use of products we use every day to issues regarding biodiversity, endangered species, climate change, tropical deforestation, agriculture, air and water pollution, energy production and use, waste disposal, and the role of politics and economics in environmental issues.

Water plays an essential role in sustaining human and ecosystem health; it also has tremendous recreational, agricultural, commercial, and industrial value. How do we as a society balance these competing needs? The purpose of this course is to explore topics related to freshwater use, access, and availability within North America.

This course will help develop a foundational understanding of how our energy system works, as well as the environmental, social, and economic implications of future energy solutions. Throughout this course, we will analyze the available technical and non-technical options that may be part of our energy future.

This course provides students with a broad, interdisciplinary understanding of sustainability in society and establishing a platform from which to further research, study, and put it into practice. Students learn to connect sustainability to real-world challenges, evaluate its claims, develop knowledge to participate in sustainability debates, and identify novel pathways towards a more sustainable society.

This course is an introduction to business and sustainability. This course explores how corporations take into account social and environmental impacts in addition to financial performance. The goal is to help students develop the skills to critically analyze these corporate activities and recognize strengths and weaknesses in different corporate strategies.

Energy production and consumption practices are critical to humanity's future. As markets embrace low-carbon, renewable sources, students will learn about the physics of energy in engineering and systems contexts, and work in teams to explore aspects of this complex transition through lenses of environmental justice, technology, politics, and economics.

This course will introduce students to different ways individuals and groups work to address social and environmental challenges. Students will explore different social and environmental problems, systems that shape them, and various types of change agents addressing them. Classes will be discussion-based to encourage critical dialogue around social change work.

This course will explore the social history of Middle Eastern (and North African) food and drink, examining records from ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, medieval cookbooks and wine poetry from Baghdad, imperial art and account books of the Ottoman palace, to modern cookbook-memoirs.

This course explores people of color environmental concerns and specifically focuses on the connection between communities of color and low-income groups and the location of hazardous waste sites.  This course also explores Native American environmental issues and the connection between the transboundary shipping of hazardous waste from developed countries to developing ones.

This course is built on the premise that, far from being a distraction from environmental degradation, engaging with art, literature, and the humanities can, in fact, enable us to be more imaginative, ethical, and effective environmental stewards. Specifically, we'll consider how this can help us think of environmental crisis anew.

In the age of climate change, environmental problems are as large and urgent as ever before. In this course, we use the lens of economics to characterize environmental problems and the theoretical and empirical impacts of possible policy solutions. Course assignments include problem sets, quizzes, and writing exercises. Class is a combination of lecture and discussion.

This course is an introduction to environmental history, which combines traditional historical methods with findings from ecology to explore how humans have transformed nature and how nature has shaped human history. It focuses on how human-nature interactions can illuminate key problems in global history (e.g. inter-scalar feedbacks, human agency).
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a social science perspective. Specific social science topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a natural science perspective. Specific natural science topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a humanities perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from an interdisciplinary perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.

This course will review the history of sustainability cultures and zero waste movements to problem solve some of the sustainability issues that we face today. The class will explore a variety of resources: 17th century receipt archives, theater records, war propaganda, scavenger hunts, current YouTube influencers, and urban sustainability documentaries.

We will examine sustainable development and globalization through the struggles with food and water scarcity and energy justice. Using lectures, films, discussions, and assignments, this course aims to foster critical thinking about how societies are organized, and to evaluate what we can contribute to the pursuit of a sustainable and just biosphere.

This course will help students begin to understand the relationships within and between different spheres of an ecosystem, develop observation skills, and learn techniques in hands-on field data collection. Throughout the course, students will learn to curate, analyze, and interpret data. Finally, students will reveal their research discoveries with a presentation.
Independent study covering different resource issues. Maximum of eight hours to be counted toward degree requirements.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a social science perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a natural science perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a humanities perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from an interdisciplinary perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.

This course examines a critical environmental issue of the 21st century:  freshwater scarcity, an issue that intersects with other environmental, economic and political issues such as food, biodiversity, trade, international security, and global justice.  Questions are raised concerning international cooperation, local-global interactions, collective action, sustainability, development, trade, North-South relations, equity, and diplomatic practice.

This course explores how the environment influences health and well-being.  In order to tackle this complex topic the physical, psychological, and social dimensions of health are considered.  The course then explores how issues like climate change, materialism, and sprawl might impact health and the potential benefits associated with sustainable lifestyles.

This course is an advanced offering on environmental politics and the environmental policy-making process.  The course will consider both processes of policy formation and implementation, placing particular emphasis on the development of alternatives to conventional regulatory practices at federal, state, and local levels of government.

Overview of historic and present-day causes of species extinction, and of biological principles central to species conservation and sustainable management of ecosystems. Topics covered include episodes of extinction and diversification over earth history; geographic distribution strategies; and sustainable use of ecosystems. Weekly recitation sections discuss material from lectures, assigned readings and films, and perform computer and gaming simulations.

Climate change is the greatest environmental and development challenge facing the world. Course will introduce students to the following: human dimensions of global climate change; key concepts and examples related to impacts, mitigation, vulnerability, resilience, and adaptation; and how government, civil society, and market actors can jointly solve climate problems related to migration, public health, and urbanization.

Nature and the environment feature prominently in the philosophy and cultural traditions of the German-speaking world. In this course we will examine ecocriticism's history and the appearance and disappearance of environmental themes in German-language literature, film, and art over the course of the last two centuries. Class taught in English.

This course explores the concept of sustainability culture and the use of social science research methods to assess cultural change here at UM. Through lectures, discussion, guest lectures, and a team-based research project this course will provide students with an opportunity to learn how to evaluate sustainability initiatives and programs.

This seminar examines how children in crisis are portrayed in picture books, Y/A fiction, fairy tales, and film. How are they represented as killers or consumers, soldiers or refugees? Do empire, frontier and classic war stories still influence narratives today? How do gender, family resilience, and terrorism figure in stories?

This course explores the climate justice movement, which frames climate change as an issue of social justice. We will learn how climate change affects people around the world differently, what the climate justice movement aims to do about that, and its relationship to the mainstream climate movement.

This course is an introduction to the role of humans in shaping the built environment. It explores physical design and cultural meaning at various scales and contexts in the landscape. We explore the power of physical design and planning to enrich the human spirit, provide functional needs, interpret cultural history, and sustain natural systems.

Many people want the things they buy to be made in just and sustainable ways, but markets comprised of profit-maximizing firms often fail to offer such options. This course examines the causes of this market failure and assesses movement organization strategies for increasing corporate responsiveness to ethical consumer demands.

Course deals with two central themes: First, environmental problems are people problems, requiring an understanding of how people think, what they care about, and the conditions under which they behave most reasonably. Second, human behavior makes the most sense when studied in the context of the environment, both present and evolutionary. This course builds a model of human nature, based upon research in the field of environmental psychology.

This course deals with how to reframe and promote a future with a restrained and austere existence.  To meet this challenge, behavior-change tools and strategies are developed. Emphasis is on informational and motivational means of changing behavior in a durable manner.

Why is climate change challenging to solve - and what can we do? This course explores the international and domestic politics of responding to global warming, one of the extraordinary challenges of our era.

This course explores what we do and why we do what we do to the world around us.  Without ignoring the theoretical, this course will focus on ethics as it bears on practical, everyday things: using energy, eating food, building houses, flying to far-away destinations, hiking in wild places, watching birds....  Our effects are far reaching: climate change, industrial agriculture and CAFOs, pollution and ecological restoration, biodiversity and species extinctions, wilderness, genetic engineering of plants and animals.  We will ask "what is a good way to live in nature?"

This course uses a case-based approach. Each case represents a specific real-world problem related to environment and sustainability in the Great Lakes region. In many studies, industrial agriculture looms large, including Lake Erie harmful algal blooms, the expansion of biofuel feedstock growth, and wildlife conservation of the Monarch butterfly.

This course explores the connections between world religions/worldviews and ecological issues. This course closely reads religious traditions and practices for their ecological practices (or lack thereof), as well as pursues conversations with members of religious communities regarding the environmental overtones of their religious faith. Also examined are new religious practices - 'dark, green religion' as some have called it - that has sprung up in support of an ecological framework.

This course will cover the concepts and practices of environmental sustainability as they pertain to the campus of this university. Students will design and conduct projects about managing this campus more sustainably than is currently practiced.

This is a project-based course that focuses on sustainability consulting for sports organizations. We will use Michigan Athletics as an example for applying key sustainability frameworks and introduce other sports examples in class. Groups will be assigned sustainability projects building off of previous teams' work on Michigan Athletics and sustainability.
Undergrads, with the guidance of a faculty advisor, participate in an internship relevant to their field of study.

This course is intended to start Honors students on their thesis projects. Students will develop a topic of interest into a research proposal. This requires identifying the topic, assessing the pertinent literature, finding a faculty sponsor, and preparing a research design. Course readings and discussions will focus on research methodology.
Independent study covering different resource issues. Maximum of eight hours to be counted toward degree requirements.

This course investigates land development in America from the perspective of political imperatives and policy frameworks at the local, state, and national levels. It leverages insights from political science, history, law, and urban planning to understand how policy does (and does not) guide land use patterns, and how it might do so differently in the future.

Most of the discussion of sustainable development in the U.S. focuses on cities. But cities depend economically and ecologically on rural communities-small towns, villages, and counties. This course focuses on what sustainable development looks like in smaller, rural communities in the U.S.

This course provides an overview of the policy and legal justifications for and institutional arrangements used to manage the use and development of land in the U.S., focusing especially on the management of privately owned land by state and local governments for environmental protection purposes.

This course focuses on the skills and strategies that can help you become a more effective leader for the environment. Students will learn about the importance of decision-making, influence, and teamwork for implementing organization change and innovation towards greater environmental stewardship.

This course will engage with the intersection of business, sustainability, and justice. It is designed to help students recognize and analyze how businesses' approaches to sustainability support and/or neglect issues of justice. The course offers students an opportunity to develop critical thinking on topics such as businesses' impact on environmental and social justice. Class sessions will be discussion-based.

This course offers an introduction to the science, policy, and social issues around ecological restoration and explores where local agriculture fits in the larger context of restoration. We examine and discuss a multitude of restoration projects - urban, rural, and natural areas - through the use of case studies, field trips, and guest lectures from local practitioners of restoration ecology. Field trips to local restoration sites will include field exercises to learn how to collect data for site inventory, monitoring, and assessing restoration success.

This course offers hands-on understanding and foundational skill-building in the principles and practices of ecological and organic farming. Based at the UM Campus Farm at Matthaei Botanical Gardens, students will meet weekly for farm walk (field-based lecture) exploring both the theory and practices associated with organic and ecological farming.

This class will investigate communication of sustainability challenges using visuals and other community-engaged methods. You'll make charts, maps, and infographics and learn new ways to engage the public in conversation about the environment using social media, and decision-support tools. You'll also deepen your understanding of how people perceive and interpret graphical representations, and learn how to make impactful data visualizations. Moreover, we will learn about decision-support tools.

Students will collaborate with peers in Bogota to explore public conversation at the intersection of poverty and environment in the US and Colombia. International student teams produce podcast episodes featuring interviews from many perspectives. Students will deepen global competencies and communication skills.

Tropical and subtropical regions are the most biologically diverse regions of our planet, but they are facing many challenges. This course will explore fundamentals of the conservation and ecology of these regions, and examine how local and global-based approaches address key issues like sustainable use, conservation, and conflicts between humans and wildlife.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a social science perspective. Specific social science topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from a humanities perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.
This special topics course seeks to examine environmental problems and issues from an interdisciplinary perspective. Specific topics will vary by term.

With the aid of the course instructor and faculty sponsor, the research plan developed in the Junior Honors Seminar is implemented and data/information is collected, analyzed, and synthesized.  An oral presentation is made and the thesis is submitted to the faculty sponsor.

This business basics course covers how to make a product or service idea real in the form of a tangible, marketable product and an organization that can produce and distribute it.  Topic areas covered include:  motivation and social purpose of entrepreneurship, market research and product development activities, people resource management, capital resources management, and go-to-market management.
This course introduces students to French language and culture with an emphasis on communication. The content-based approach integrates grammar with functional use.

The sequence of FRENCH 101/102 presents the essentials of French grammar, vocabulary, and culture needed to communicate in French at a moderate speed. Vocabulary and structures are practiced through communicative activities stressing listening and speaking. Authentic documents are used to develop reading skills. Cultural awareness and listening skills are also developed through listening and video materials.

The sequence of FRENCH 101/102 presents the essentials of French grammar, vocabulary, and culture needed to communicate in French at a moderate speed. Vocabulary/structures are practiced through communicative activities stressing listening and speaking. Authentic documents are used to develop reading skills. Cultural awareness/listening skills are also developed through listening/video materials.
A refresher course for students with previous training in French, but not ready for a second-year course.
Accelerated course designed to develop reading and translation competence in French.

FRENCH 231 develops and refines listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills; provides strategies for effective communication and reading; reviews and adds to previously learned grammatical structures and uses; develops an awareness of French-speaking cultures; utilizes technology to help with the study of French and to have greater access to Francophone cultural documents.

FRENCH 232 uses literature, magazine articles, videos, and songs to explore the history of France and several Francophone countries. Students are expected to review and learn various grammatical elements and vocabulary in order to participate in classroom activities and discussions. Linguistically, it focuses on supporting opinions, making comparisons, hypothesizing, and composing sophisticated sentences.

Through current events and their historical background, this course focuses on some concepts essential to French-Francophone Studies: slavery, colonialism, decolonization, migration, race relations, globalization, gender and sexuality. While stressing a communicative approach, the content of this course will be presented with a review and expansion of grammatical structures.
Intensive study of a selected topic in the cultures and societies of French-speaking peoples, taught in English using translated materials.

This course examines a series of remarkable episodes in modern French painting, from the establishment of an official, state-sponsored form of Classicism to the succession of movements that emerged in opposition to official art.  The course is also designed to encourage close readings of images within the parameters of their historical contexts and of recent critical debates.
Intensive study of cultural productions and social issues in French-speaking societies related to issues of race or ethnicity, taught in English using translated materials.

Intensive study of a topic, theme, or genre in the literatures and other cultural productions of French-speaking peoples, providing an introduction to the methods and practice of literary and cultural study in the French language and opportunities for development of linguistic proficiency beyond the 4th semester level.

Intensive study of a topic in the culture of French-speaking peoples with emphasis on film, television, and other modern media, providing an introduction to the methods and practice of film and media study in the French language and  opportunities for development of linguistic proficiency beyond the fourth-semester level.

Intensive study of a topic in the culture, politics, and structures of French-speaking societies providing an introduction to the methods and practice of cultural and social study in the French language and opportunities for development of linguistic proficiency beyond the 4th semester level.
Intensive practice in the creation, production and performance of culture through the French language providing opportunities for development of linguistic proficiency beyond the 4th semester level.
This course is designed for students interested in understanding the professional world (business, medical fields, education, law) in connection with the French-speaking world.
This course is designed to provide maximum conversation practice based on topical French and/or Francophone films along with related readings.

This is a three-credit course for the academic work associated with an internship that involves the extensive use of French in a location in which French is a primary language. Course requirements consist of oral and written assignments, pre- and post-internship meetings, and presentations. Aside from these requirements, the class does not meet.
Introduction to the discipline of phonetics in addition to practical exercises and practice to refine one's accent.

This course focuses on textual interpretation and written production. Students will acquire stylistic, narrative, rhetorical and prosodic tools indispensable in textual analysis and written activities.

This course introduces the main concepts and methods of analysis in linguistic theory focusing on French and related languages. The analysis of sounds (phonetics) and sound systems (phonology), word formation (morphology), sentence structure (syntax), and meaning (semantics) is the focus of the course. Additionally, the intersection of language and society (socio-linguistics) is treated throughout.

The French revolution of 1789 announced the beginning of a new age in which established social and political traditions were to be swept away before the bracing winds of cultural novelty and political experimentation. Using a variety of sources--biography, historical documents, novels, and recent studies--this class explores the social and political history of France's revolutionary century, paying special attention to its resonance beyond its borders.

In the fall of 2005, people all over the world were shocked to see images broadcast on television of young men in France burning cars and schools in their own neighborhoods and battling with heavily armored police on the outskirts of many French cities. With the help of autobiographies, novels, and works of history written by French people who lived in metropolitan France, as well as Senegal, Algeria, and Martinique, we examine the painful trajectory of French history across this period.

This course focuses on Parisian visual culture from 1848 to the end of the nineteenth century. Its principal objective is to evaluate Realist and Impressionist painting in relation to new forms of print media, emergent forms of popular and mass culture, and an unstable social and political landscape.

Since the Roman conquest of Carthage, North Africa has been a major center of Jewish life. As a Diasporic community connecting Afro-Arab and European cultures, Jews have complicated how we perceive the colonized subject. Students examine how Jewish history helps to deconstruct divisions between the Orient and Occident and North/South.

Readings and topical studies relating to French speaking cultures (in Europe, Africa, North America, and Indian Ocean) not addressed in other courses, as well as to aspects of French and Francophone culture that may require special treatment.

Study of the French presence in Asia and the Pacific, including Indochina, Vietnam, India and the Indian Ocean, French Melanesia and Polynesia. Topics could also include French encounters with other societies and cultures in Asia and the Pacific in places France did not establish a colonial presence. Taught in French.
Introduction to the history and legacy of French presence in the Caribbean, on-going relations between the two regions, and the francophone culture that has resulted from shared traditions.
Study of the philosophical trends, literature, culture, and artistic productions of France spanning the mid-nineteenth century to the present.
Study of cinematic expression in France treating the country's intimate relationship with film's history, development, and critical appreciation.
Examination of the structures of French society as well as social theories that have emerged in France.
Introduction to issues of gender and sexuality as they have arisen in France and the particular formulation they have received there.

This course is designed to familiarize the students with the language of business transactions in France. It deals with both written and spoken commercial French. It is partly built around a fictitious company  whose activities are divided into themes dealing with various aspects of the business world.
Preparation for internship experience; completion of internship in a Francophone country; follow-up class upon return.
First semester of supervised independent study for the purpose of completing an honors thesis in French.
Supervised independent study leading to the following:  completion of an honors thesis; a program of selected readings and conferences, term papers, or reports; and written examinations.

In this engaging course, students learn how to assess film, television, and digital media, and ways that style shapes the meanings of the media that surround us in everyday life. Students learn critical vocabulary and methods of media analysis.

This course introduces students to the ways in which cinema functions as a form for artistic expression. It examines cinematically specific structures (time and space manipulation, montage, etc.) as well as film's relationship to other artistic enterprises such as theater, literature, painting, etc.
This course covers specific media production topics, allowing students from all majors to gain experience in an aspect of making media.

This course teaches students how timeless dramatic principles function in feature films, television shows, and new media. Through weekly exercises, students learn first-hand how the elements of storytelling (characterization, point-of-view, subtext, symbolism, dramatic irony, etc.) translate to filmed narratives in ways different from fiction and the stage.
Course topics vary. Course topics will focus primarily on experiential learning in the field of film, television and media.

This course explores the concepts of race and ethnicity through film productions and their complex histories. It focuses on Jewish cultures across the globe and how their experiences have been represented on the screen. We view American immigrant cinema; Nazi propaganda film; Holocaust cinema; and Israeli and Palestinian films.

This course addresses the role of film and television as popular media and serves as an introduction to cultural studies. Students will be taught to read and analyze specific popular films, genres, or figures; at the same time, the course introduces broader issues in cultural studies. Content varies by term and instructor.

What is cinema? What should film do? How do spectators perceive and understand projected moving images? This course examines the writings of a number of classical film theorists, working to understand, apply, and interrogate their respective arguments to these types of questions in relation to a series of selected films.

This course is a hands-on survey course in media production introducing television, digital video, and film. Students gain firsthand experience in strategies and techniques of scripting and pre-production, production, and post-production, as well as a fundamental understanding of the aesthetics and processes of film, video, and television production.

This course familiarizes students with dramatic narrative movie production from interpreting the screenplay through location production techniques and post-production. It provides solid understanding of how standard movie production processes and techniques are used to effectively communicate ideas in Dramatic Narrative productions. Students produce and participate in short film productions.

This course teaches the theoretical, aesthetic and technical principles of making a documentary, focusing on knowing what makes a story compelling and how to convey the ideas visually. The shaping of story, creating powerful images, using sound, script writing, narration, and editing with Final Cut Pro is explored.

Building on previous television experience, this course is designed to focus on the relationship between technique and content in television programs. Students receive continued hands-on experience in multi-camera studio television production through a series of increasingly complex directing projects.
This is a workshop-based course designed to teach specific topics, approaches, and subjects in media production.
This course provides intermediate experience in special production topics. Film, video, television and/or digital production may focus on a particular subject area and/or approach to the medium.

This course encourages consideration of alternative and hybrid practices in moving image and sound production, examining production and presentation tools used to make compelling media projects. Students write and produce works for a variety of settings in a range of media including 16mm film, HD video, and other resources.

This course introduces new media processes and practices, engaging with an array of materials, hardware and software to produce projects for a variety of platforms. Starting with 2D animation, we consider current strategies to produce media, its evolution, and how contemporary new media interface with current cinematic and artistic practices.

Filmmakers learn about filmmaking by watching films. This course reverse engineers movies to understand how they were produced. The goal is to learn from a finished film how the scenes were produced in front of the camera and microphone and how the captured material was edited.

This fast-paced adaptation course encompasses both screenwriting and production, taking published works of short fiction by contemporary authors and turning these short stories into short screenplays and then completed short films.

This course teaches students to write a feature-length screenplay.  Students begin with the development of a concept, proceed to writing a treatment, and then spend the majority of the semester working on the full script.  Students will read and critique each other's work.

This course teaches students to write full length teleplays for various small-screen formats. The class has rotating formats so students will focus on one genre or serial format during a given semester, such as sit-coms, dramas, soap-operas, etc.

During four decades of Communist Party rule, the film industries of Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and the former Yugoslavia were under state control. One positive result of this was ample funding for serious films about social and political topics. In certain thematic areas, particularly those dealing with racial and ethnic intolerance and with the plight of women in patriarchal societies, filmmakers in East Central Europe were often able to be more incisive, frank and provocative than is often the case in profit-driven Hollywood film. Talented and committed filmmakers crafted powerful films which the regimes had no ideological grounds to suppress; this tradition of critical filmmaking has continued into the post-Communist period. The films we study concern the Holocaust, women's lives under state socialism, and the ethno-nationalism that led to the wars in the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s. We view and discuss fourteen films from East Central Europe dealing with the above issues, considering the artistic structure of the films as well.

Course covers Polish cinema from WWII to the present, tracing the development of film styles in the context of the historical, political, and cultural features of Polish society, with focus on the use of realist norms, intricate symbolism, and absurdist allegory to critique the loss of civic values under Communism.

This course examines the history of Italian Americans' media representation from silent and early gangster films to The Jersey Shore. It also explores how the Hollywood industries have historically translated stereotypes about Italians' national, racial, and ethnic difference into appealing representations to achieve popular consensus.

This course is a fun multi-cam television production class open to all students. Students create short pilot episodes for any genre of television including comedy skits, sitcoms, news, sports, talk shows, variety shows, music shows etc. The shows developed in class are part of the WOLV-TV slate of shows.

Course covers the history of Ukrainian cinema from the 1920s to the present, with emphasis on four periods of revolutionary developments: Soviet montage (1920s-30s), Socialist Realism (1930s-50s), poetic cinema (1960s), and new documentary and hybrid film genres emerging during the recent war (2014-2022).
This course provides an overview of the history of Iranian cinema, with an eye for identifying the major trends, genres, and filmmakers from the 1960s to the present day.

The last century has known no shortage or horrors: genocide, world wars, climate catastrophes, authoritarian regimes, global pandemic. This course examines the ways in which Armenian filmmakers -- no strangers to disaster -- chose to transmute the calamities of the last century into mysterious, surprising, and haunting art.
An introduction to German cinema and its cultural background from the beginning to the present, with emphasis on the classical period (ca. 1918 to 1938) and the modern (post-1965) resurgence.

This interdisciplinary course explores the fascist-era cinemas of Germany, Spain, Italy, and Japan.  It focuses on a set of common themes to identify both commonalities and specificities of a given context or historical moment.

This course will consider various ideas and imaginaries of Detroit through an investigation of the way that the city has been represented in film and other visual media, including television, music videos, photography, painting, and art installations.

The screening of moving images encompasses a long and fascinating history that begins even before the emergence of cinema. International in scope and intermedial in approach, this course examines the diversity of screen practices that preceded the introduction of synchronized sound at the end of the 1920s.

This course introduces the history of cinema from its technological and cultural origins in the late nineteenth century to the global impact of the French New Wave. Objectives include orienting students to a wide range of cinema and illuminating the development of narrative form and film style.

This course examines development of cinema during a period characterized by significant changes in film form style and important industrial and technological developments. It considers international dimensions of these changes, their specific national and institutional contexts, and questions of historical method in film scholarship of this period to current trends.

This course offers a historical survey of U.S. television from the late 1940s to the mid-2010s, examining how historically specific economic, political, and regulatory forces have shaped the medium?s development. We will also consider how television programs have reflected, reassessed, criticized, and/or celebrated social and cultural transformations.

This course is a tour through the history of non-fiction film. From the early "actualities" to contemporary works of digital multi-format cinema, we'll explore the evolution, context, and impact of various narrative and aesthetic documentary forms like: propaganda, experimental, direct cinema, POV and found footage films, civil rights, and activism.
Focusing on the post-WWII period, this course looks at Italian cinema from a number of perspectives: political, commercial, social, and aesthetic.

This course addresses the role of film and television as popular media and serves as an introduction to cultural studies. Students will be taught to read and analyze specific popular films, genres, or figures; at the same time, the course introduces broader issues in cultural studies.

This course addresses the role of film and television as popular media and serves as an introduction to cultural studies. Students will be taught to read and analyze specific popular films, genres, or figures; at the same time, the course introduces broader issues in cultural studies.

This course explores how different theories and methods of analysis built on structural and post-structural presuppositions and paradigms have influenced recent film theory, its consideration of narrative practice, the psychological experience of viewing, the construction of moving image representations, and the impact of technology on aesthetic practice.

Introduction to various methodologies in study of commercial television programming; semiotic, linguistic, rhetorical, cultural, etc. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed upon inquiry into what television is saying and how messages are represented for mass comprehension.

This course traces a history of image making by Jews in twentieth-century Europe and the U.S. While Jewish photographers participated in many different aspects of photography, particular attention will be given to documentary photography.

Examining the role that film, television, video games, and other media play in shaping our sense of global, national, and local cultures and identities, this course will focus on the role of global media institutions and how diverse audiences use global media to negotiate with issues of cultural identity.

With a focus on theory and craft, this class explores editing as the third and final authoring of a motion picture. Emphasizing technique and storytelling over software, this class initially challenges students to consider the power of the "cut" and progress into more advanced editing methods and considerations.

This advanced course is designed to teach the theoretical, aesthetic and technical principles of making compelling non-fiction productions. The class includes readings and viewing of clips to investigate current and past issues in non-fiction production that include documentary form, objectivity in documentary production, ethics, and representation.
This is an advanced course in television production focusing on a multi-camera studio or location production. Possible topics may include Situation Comedy or Live Event Production.

From television's earliest history, sketch comedy has been an integral part of the television landscape. Through screenings, readings, discussion, guest speakers, and productions Television Sketch Comedy explores this perennial form. Students collaborate on original sketch comedy programs in a variety of forms.

An advanced course in special production topics that may include film, video, television and/or digital production within a particular subject area and/or approach to the medium. It also may focus on collaborations with other courses or units.

In this course, students research new media practice, new software and hardware, and new presentation methods. Rotating topics include: special effects for cinema; audio/visual performance; web-based serial production; and 2D digital animation. The course culminates in the design and production of individual or team-based final projects.

This capstone course prepares screenwriting sub-majors to pitch concepts for feature films and to take meetings with industry producers and executives. Students create and deliver 1-minute, 5-minute, and 15-minute pitches for original feature films. Students also create a portfolio page for a directory which will be distributed to industry professionals.

This course is an intermediate course in the art and practice of screenwriting. It stresses creative dramatic writing and focuses on critical tools for rewriting. Each student is expected to write or rewrite a feature length screenplay.

This course offers students the opportunity to conceive and develop their own television series, from the creation of a "pitch deck" to the completion of a full-length spec script of the pilot episode.
In this course, students will make music videos, with permission and active participation from the musicians whose work they are expressing visually.

TV Pilot is a production/writing course. Students work collaboratively to produce a full-length original pilot conceived in 411 Writing for Television II. This course prepares you for both creative and crew positions in the TV and Film industries.

Film is by nature a collaborative art. This practicum is designed to teach students how to collaborate. Via the screenwriting and production processes, students learn to appreciate, respect and gain understanding of their fellow students' crafts, all the while building upon their own skills and abilities.

An advanced screenwriting course that provides individual and small group instruction to select students who have completed basic and intermediate screenwriting. Students write a final draft of a revised original screenplay and a first draft of a new screenplay.

The Screen Arts Mavericks and Makers Collections in the UM Special Collections Research Center is a major resource of important film and media makers. Students in this laboratory course develop proficiency with primary-source archival research while using unique materials found only in these collections to create new knowledge.

This class explores the evolution and forms of specific national or regional cinema in terms of their stylistic, socio-political, economic, and technological dimensions. Also, close study of the development of a cinema (e.g. Japanese, British, Indian) or of a film movement (e.g. Italian Neorealism, French New Wave).

Bollywood today signifies more than cinema, it is a global culture industry that encompasses everything from dance, music and fashion to food and yoga. The course will examine this massive culture industry and its circulation in the global space as a unique cultural form.
Studies in various film topics, such as silent film, women and film, German Expressionism, and Latin-American film.

This course traces impact of technological innovations like sound, color, and wide screen on the history of motion picture and the evolution beyond cinema of new digital technology, virtual reality, and multi-media performances. It examines the aesthetics of technology and how technology through art influences individual psychology and society.

This course offers an in-depth exploration of feminist and queer theories that address film in relation to gender. Discussion focuses on contemporary feminist and queer scholarship that draws upon a variety of viewpoints, including psychoanalysis, cultural theory, postmodernism, historical research and ideological theory.

In this course students work, under careful supervision, in some part of the media industry. Students work in some aspect of preproduction, production, or postproduction, in the creative or business areas of media, documenting their experiences and learning in a journal that must be submitted for final credit.

Explores the impact of global trade and cultural exchange on audiovisual media during different periods in media history.   Topics rotate.  Possible topics include international film co-productions, censorship and state regulation, the transnational transmission of television, and translation and the politics of reception.
This course is a year-long workshop led by a faculty member which includes all seniors writing Honors theses, or completing Honors creative production projects in Film, Television, and Media.

Independent study on a subject to be determined by student in conjunction with a faculty member.  Does not count toward concentration requirements.  Must be approved by Department in term prior to enrollment.  In exceptional cases, students can petition for enrollment during current term.
Directed Study on a subject to be determined by student in conjunction with a faculty member.

This course explores the ways in which ideas, people, goods, services, diseases, and natural resources have flowed across political, economic, societal, and cultural borders during human history, examines the consequences of those flows, and provides context for how these topics can be the basis of a professional career.
Directed study and readings related to Human Geography.
The completion of the content of GERMAN 101 and GERMAN 102 in one semester.

GERMAN 101 is an introductory course for students who have not previously studied German. Learning a new language for the first time is exciting and fun, and the course curriculum and materials focus on engaging students' interest, creativity, and sense of humor. The course focuses systematically on the concurrent development of students' ability to understand spoken and written German and to speak and write German themselves, and on exposing students to a broad range of aspects of German culture. While children may be good at picking up a second language when living in the culture, adults are much better at learning languages in the classroom. This course aims to take advantage of this by helping students to develop effective language learning strategies and by providing students with a wide range of tools and resources to help them to learn the language.
